questions.q: How should a licensee describe a home "built to code"?
choices: Built to the highest quality available
Built to the minimum legal standards
Inspected and warranted by the city
questions.explain: Building codes set minimum standards; meeting code doesn't mean high quality.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Codes, standards and the people who enforce them

questions.q: Which body issues permits for electrical and gas work in most of BC?
questions.explain: Technical Safety BC licenses contractors and issues electrical and gas permits, separate from building permits.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Codes, standards and the people who enforce them

questions.q: Which city has its own building bylaw instead of using the BC Building Code?
questions.explain: Vancouver has the Vancouver Building By-law (VBBL).
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Codes, standards and the people who enforce them

questions.q: Which of these needs no electrical permit?
choices: Adding a new circuit for a hot tub
Running wiring to a new garage
questions.explain: Swapping fixtures, switches or thermostats doesn't need a permit; new wiring does.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Codes, standards and the people who enforce them

questions.q: What crisis led to the Homeowner Protection Act in 1998?
questions.explain: Poorly built and waterproofed buildings caused about $4 billion of damage: the leaky condo crisis.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the HPA's three core requirements?
choices: Homes must be built in concrete
questions.explain: The HPA requires licensing, registration and warranty insurance. It doesn't dictate building materials.

questions.q: How much experience does an applicant for a residential builder licence need?
questions.explain: 24 months managing or supervising residential construction within the previous 5 years.

questions.q: The online New Homes Registry covers homes registered after which date?
questions.explain: For homes registered before November 19, 2007, contact Licensing and Consumer Services.

questions.q: A house got its occupancy permit 7 years ago and has had three owners. Is it a "new home" under the HPA?
choices: No, only the first buyer is covered
No, after 5 years it's a resale
Only if the builder still owns it
questions.explain: The 10-year period runs from the occupancy permit regardless of how many times it's sold.

questions.q: Which renovation makes a house a "new home" under the HPA?
choices: A full kitchen and bathroom renovation
questions.explain: More than 75% of the structure above the foundation removed or replaced (or a new foundation with 50% new structure).

questions.q: A new foundation is poured and new structure (with the foundation) makes up what share for substantial reconstruction?
questions.explain: A new foundation plus new structural components making up 50% of the finished structure.

questions.q: A licensee listed a fully rebuilt house without warranty insurance. What was the outcome in the case discussed?
questions.explain: The listing licensee was fined $1,200; they didn't know substantial rebuilds count as new homes.

questions.q: Why was a buyer's licensee suspended 7 days in a warranty case?
choices: For charging too high a commission
For never asking about warranty insurance
For listing without the seller's consent
For refusing to show the property
questions.explain: She didn't ask about mandatory warranty insurance or put it in the contract; the home had none.

questions.q: How long must a warranty cover defects in the building envelope?
questions.explain: 2 years materials and labour, 5 years envelope (including water penetration), 10 years structural.

questions.q: How long must a warranty cover structural defects?
questions.explain: Structural defects: 10 years.

questions.q: What is the minimum claim limit for a strata unit?
choices: The lesser of $50,000 or its value
The lesser of $100,000 or its value
The lesser of $200,000 or its value
questions.explain: Strata units: not less than the lesser of $100,000 or the value. Fee simple: $200,000.

questions.q: What is the minimum claim limit for a fee simple home?
choices: The lesser of $100,000 or its value
The lesser of $200,000 or its value
The greater of $200,000 or its value
questions.explain: Not less than the lesser of $200,000 or the value of the home.

questions.q: Who can get an owner-builder authorization?
choices: A company building homes to resell
An individual building for own use
A developer building a small duplex
questions.explain: It must be an individual who intends to live in the home, not a company.

questions.q: How long must an owner-builder live in the home without renting it?
questions.explain: At least one year from occupancy, with no renting in that time.

questions.q: When can an owner-builder first sell the home?
choices: Any time while it's under construction
questions.explain: No sale during construction or within 12 months of the occupancy permit.

questions.q: A later owner sells an owner-built home 6 years after occupancy. What's required?
choices: Nothing, since they didn't build it
questions.explain: Any sale within 10 years needs disclosure saying whether warranty insurance exists.

questions.q: Who licenses home inspectors in BC?
questions.explain: Home inspectors are licensed by Consumer Protection BC.

questions.q: Your buyer asks you to recommend an inspector. What's best practice?
choices: Give the name of your usual inspector
Give at least three names to choose from
Book and pay for one yourself
questions.explain: Provide at least three names and let the buyer choose; don't steer them.

questions.q: An inspector pays you a referral fee. What must you do?
choices: Nothing; it's a private business matter
Disclose it to the client in writing
Split it evenly with your client
Refund it to the inspector at once
questions.explain: Rules s.56 requires written disclosure of remuneration from a referral.

questions.q: A buyer refuses an inspection. What should their licensee do?
choices: Insist and refuse to write the offer
Tell the seller to fix everything
questions.explain: Recommend it, and if declined, document the decision.

questions.q: How is floor area of an attached townhouse measured at a shared wall?
choices: To the inside face of the wall
To the centre line of the wall
To the outside face of the wall
The wall is not included at all
questions.explain: Measure to the exterior of walls and to the centre line of party walls.

questions.q: When does a floor count as "above grade"?
choices: When most of it is above ground
When it is entirely above ground
When it has a separate entrance
questions.explain: Only if it's entirely above the ground.

questions.q: Which is included in finished floor area?
choices: A loft reached only by ladder
questions.explain: Garages, unfinished areas and ladder-only spaces are excluded.

questions.q: A suite measures 90 m². About how many square feet is that?
What's the actual size of a metric "2×4" stud?
questions.explain: About 38 × 89 mm.

questions.q: What's the difference between dampproofing and waterproofing?
choices: They are two words for the same thing
One slows moisture; one stops water
Waterproofing is only used on roofs
Dampproofing is the stronger of the two
questions.explain: Dampproofing slows moisture; waterproofing resists water under pressure.

questions.q: Why do many homes in Richmond and Delta have no basements?
choices: Basements are too costly to heat
questions.explain: High water tables make basements impractical.

questions.q: On which side of the insulation does the vapour barrier go?
choices: Neither; it goes in the attic
questions.explain: On the warm side, to stop indoor moisture reaching the cold parts of the wall.

questions.q: What framing method do most BC houses use?
questions.explain: Each floor is built as a platform and the next walls go on top.

questions.q: Which construction type is most common for mid- and high-rise buildings?
questions.explain: Concrete, with about a 2-hour fire rating.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Construction types for bigger buildings

questions.q: What is a known drawback of wood frame construction in taller buildings?
choices: It is the most costly type
It has no fire rating at all
questions.explain: Wood shrinks as it dries, so detailing must allow for movement.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Construction types for bigger buildings

questions.q: Why do rain screen walls perform better on the coast than face-sealed walls?
choices: They use a much thicker coat of stucco
An air gap lets water drain and dry
They are built with no windows at all
They are built with no vapour barrier
questions.explain: Face-sealing relies on a perfect seal; rain screens manage water that gets in.

questions.q: Which barrier must be continuous, with every gap sealed?
questions.explain: The air barrier must be continuous; vapour barrier continuity is less critical.

questions.q: Remedial envelope work above what cost per suite generally needs an envelope consultant?
questions.explain: More than $2,000 per suite.

questions.q: What's the difference between cedar shakes and cedar shingles?
choices: Shakes are sawn; shingles are split
Shakes are split; shingles are sawn
questions.explain: Shakes are split (rough); shingles are sawn (smooth).

questions.q: What is the minimum slope for asphalt shingles?
questions.explain: Asphalt shingles need at least a 4:12 slope.

questions.q: What does a zinc strip near the ridge of a shingled roof do?
questions.explain: Zinc washes down the roof and discourages moss.

questions.q: Why must vinyl siding be nailed loosely?
choices: So it can be removed for painting
So it can expand and contract
To let water in behind it
questions.explain: Vinyl moves with temperature; tight nailing causes buckling.

questions.q: What do weep holes in brick veneer do?
choices: Hold the bricks to the frame
questions.explain: They let water behind the brick drain out, about every 2 feet along the base.

questions.q: Which window is hinged at the top and opens outward?
questions.explain: Awning windows hinge at the top; casements at the side; hoppers at the bottom.

questions.q: When was UFFI banned in Canada?
questions.explain: Urea formaldehyde foam insulation was banned in December 1980.

questions.q: What does a higher R-value mean?
choices: Walls that dry out more quickly
questions.explain: R-value measures thermal resistance; higher is better insulation.

questions.q: What's the efficiency of a modern high-efficiency gas furnace?
questions.explain: Old units 50–60%, mid-efficiency at least 80%, high-efficiency about 95%.

questions.q: Above what level does Health Canada recommend radon remediation?
questions.explain: 200 Bq/m³ (within 2 years); above 600, within 1 year.

questions.q: A seller knows their basement tests at 350 Bq/m³. What must their licensee do?
choices: Disclose it only if the buyer asks
Disclose it only in the Interior
questions.explain: BCFSA treats radon over 200 Bq/m³ as a material latent defect.

questions.q: What is the most common radon fix?
questions.explain: A pipe and fan draw radon from under the slab and vent it outside.

questions.q: Why might upper floors of a tall building have high radon?
questions.explain: Warm air rising through shafts can carry radon up: the stack effect.

questions.q: A renovated 120 m² house must have at least what electrical service?
questions.explain: New or substantially renovated homes over 80 m² need at least 100 amps.

questions.q: Which is usually more costly to upgrade in an older home?
choices: The size of the electrical service
The label on the main breaker
questions.explain: Adding circuits and outlets usually means opening walls.

questions.q: A pre-1950 house has two-hole outlets and no ground wire. What wiring is it likely?
questions.explain: Knob and tube: two wires, no ground.

questions.q: What is required to make aluminum wiring safe?
choices: Replacing all of it with copper
questions.explain: Use CO/ALR-rated devices and anti-oxidant on joints.

questions.q: What's the typical life of a galvanized water supply system?
questions.explain: 30 to 50 years; it corrodes from the inside.

questions.q: A rural buyer asks if the well has enough water. What should you do?
choices: Assure them it has always been fine
Recommend testing and a subject clause
Tell them wells never run dry
Ask the seller to sign a guarantee
questions.explain: Never represent water sufficiency; use well reports and quality/quantity tests.

questions.q: How far from the house must a septic tank be?
questions.explain: At least ten feet away.

questions.q: Septic systems installed after May 31, 2005 must have what?
choices: A connection to the municipal sewer
questions.explain: Installed by an authorized person, with records filed with the health authority.

questions.q: How high should a deck guard be, and how small the gaps?
questions.explain: About 42 inches high, with gaps under 4 inches.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Safety details and building styles

questions.q: What are the LEED certification levels?
questions.explain: LEED: Certified, Silver, Gold, Platinum.

questions.q: What does the R-2000 standard require for air quality?
choices: No windows that can be opened
Solar panels installed on the roof
questions.explain: Air-tight homes need controlled ventilation, typically a heat recovery ventilator.

questions.q: Do appraisers need a licence under the Real Estate Services Act?
questions.explain: Appraisers are exempt; most belong to professional bodies like the AIC.

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason real estate needs appraisals?
questions.explain: Real estate is unique and trades rarely, unlike identical commodities.

questions.q: What is the AIC's designation for appraisers of all property types?
questions.explain: AACI covers all property types; CRA is residential.

questions.q: A seller won't take less than $1.1M; a buyer will pay up to $1.2M. What is the $1.1M?
questions.explain: The seller's minimum is the floor price; the buyer's maximum is the ceiling.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Floor price, ceiling price and the deal

questions.q: Which value ignores a particular owner's personal circumstances?
questions.explain: Market value is what the market as a whole would pay.

questions.q: An appraisal for a capital gains calculation values the property as of 2015. What is that date called?
questions.explain: The effective date can be in the past (estates, expropriation, capital gains, fire loss).

questions.q: Two identical buildings: one has a long lease at below-market rent. Why might values differ?
questions.explain: The appraiser values the legal interest, including leases and financing.

questions.q: What is the first step of the appraisal process?
questions.explain: Define the problem: client, use, purpose, value type, effective date, rights.

questions.q: In reconciliation, how does the appraiser reach a final value?
questions.explain: Reconciliation weighs each approach's reliability; it isn't simple averaging.

questions.q: Which type of appraisal report is the most detailed?
questions.explain: Narrative reports are full written reports; form reports are fill-in-the-blanks.

questions.q: A neighbour paid well above market to expand their yard. What is this buyer called?
questions.explain: A special purchaser's price may not reflect market value.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Conditions of the sale matter

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the highest and best use tests?
questions.explain: Legal, physical, financial and maximally productive.

questions.q: How is land "ripe for development" usually valued?
choices: Cost approach on the old house
questions.explain: Finished project value minus all development costs leaves the land value.

questions.q: Which approach suits a church with no sales or rents to compare?
questions.explain: Special-purpose properties with no market data suit the cost approach.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · The three approaches at a glance

questions.q: Which principle underlies the direct comparison approach?
questions.explain: A buyer won't pay more than the cost of an equally good substitute.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · The three approaches at a glance

questions.q: In Cantwell v. Petersen, why was the appraiser liable?
choices: For charging too much for the report
For missing dry rot and insects
For delivering the report very late
For using the wrong appraisal form
questions.explain: The appraiser missed obvious dry rot and insect damage that buyers relied on.

questions.q: What did Bourne and Cox v. Martin show about licensees?
choices: They can't be liable for pricing
questions.explain: The licensee underpriced lots that were soon resold for far more and was held liable.

questions.q: What margin of appraisal error is usually considered reasonable?
questions.explain: 5–10% is generally reasonable.

questions.q: Can a disclaimer in a report excuse an appraiser's negligence?
choices: Only if signed by the client
questions.explain: Disclaimers can't excuse negligence.

questions.q: What is a key weakness of automated valuation models?
choices: They are slow and costly to run
They can't see condition or upgrades
They must be signed by an appraiser
They only work for vacant land
questions.explain: AVMs miss condition, renovations and unique features.

questions.q: Why are current listings weak evidence of market value?
choices: They're too recent to be reliable
questions.explain: Listing prices are usually higher than what properties sell for.

questions.q: What's the weakness of declared values from Land Title records?
choices: The values are always set too high
They don't show the sale's circumstances
They're only available for strata units
They're kept secret from the public
questions.explain: A related-party sale at a low price looks like any other.

questions.q: What does "recent" mean when choosing comparables?
questions.explain: There's no fixed period; it's the time over which conditions stayed stable.

questions.q: Should an appraiser use the CPI to update a two-year-old sale?
questions.explain: Real estate doesn't move with general price indices.

questions.q: For houses, which lot dimension usually affects value most?
questions.explain: Frontage usually matters more than depth or area.

questions.q: A comparable has a fireplace; the subject doesn't. What adjustment is made?
choices: Add its value to the subject
Subtract its value from the comp
Add its value to the comp
questions.explain: Comp superior → subtract from the comparable's price.

questions.q: The subject has a garage; the comparable doesn't. What adjustment?
questions.explain: Comp inferior → add to the comparable's price.

questions.q: Which comparable is usually the best evidence?
choices: The one with the highest sale price
The one with the fewest adjustments
The one that sold the earliest
The one with the largest lot size
questions.explain: The fewer the adjustments, the better the comparable.

questions.q: A comp gets +$500,000 for view and −$500,000 for size. Why is this a problem?
choices: It is not a problem at all
questions.explain: Net is zero, but large gross adjustments show it isn't really comparable.

questions.q: As a rough guide, net adjustments shouldn't exceed what share of a comp's price?
questions.explain: About 20%, with possible exceptions for financing adjustments.

questions.q: Comp sold $870,000; needs $8,000 paint and has a lot worth $15,000 less. Adjusted price?
questions.explain: Both are inferior features, so add: $870,000 + $8,000 + $15,000 = $893,000.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Worked example: a three-comparable grid

questions.q: A comp sold with a vendor take-back at 4% when the market was 6%. How is it adjusted?
questions.explain: Cheap financing inflated the price, so adjust down to the cash-equivalent price.

questions.q: A company sold houses to its employees at a discount. Can these sales be comps?
choices: Yes, they are recent arm's-length sales
Yes, if each is adjusted by 10%
Only when using the cost approach
questions.explain: Sales with a special relationship aren't market evidence.

questions.q: Two condos in different buildings have identical floor plans. What else must be similar?
choices: The ages of the unit owners
questions.explain: Similarity includes common facilities, fees and what they cover, bylaws and the strata's finances.

questions.q: Why is the cost approach rarely used for a single strata unit?
choices: The whole building must be costed
It always gives too low a value
It's banned by the Strata Property Act
questions.explain: You'd need to cost the entire project and allocate it, which isn't practical.

questions.q: A 15,000 sq ft warehouse is most like a sale at $340/sq ft. What value is indicated?
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Income property by units of comparison

questions.q: Are corner lots always worth more than interior lots?
choices: No, it depends on the market
questions.explain: There's no fixed rule; light and width vs noise and privacy.

questions.q: When does direct comparison work poorly?
choices: When there are few recent sales
questions.explain: It needs enough recent, similar sales.

questions.q: How do most licensees treat comparables in a CMA?
choices: Exact dollar adjustments to the cent
questions.explain: CMAs are mostly qualitative.

questions.q: How many comparables does a typical CMA use?
questions.explain: Usually three to five.

questions.q: Which cost does the cost approach normally use?
questions.explain: Current prices, for a modern equivalent (replacement), not an exact replica.

questions.q: How is site value estimated in the cost approach?
questions.explain: Land can't be manufactured, so site value comes from comparable land sales.

questions.q: A 2,400 sq ft house; similar homes cost $280/sq ft to build. Replacement cost new?
When does cost roughly equal value?
choices: When the building is the HBU
questions.explain: Only when the building conforms to market demand: highest and best use.

questions.q: Cost new $800,000; effective age 10; economic life 50. Depreciated cost?
Why use effective age rather than actual age in the age-life method?
questions.explain: Effective age reflects renovations and condition.

questions.q: Sale $1.2M, land $800K, cost new $500K, age 10. Annual depreciation rate?
questions.explain: Building = $400K; lost $100K = 20% over 10 years = 2% a year.

questions.q: A house is next to a new rail line. What type of depreciation is this?
questions.explain: External depreciation is outside the property and always incurable.

questions.q: A poor floor plan that would cost more to fix than it adds is what?
questions.explain: An outdated design not worth fixing is functional incurable.

questions.q: How is curable depreciation measured?
questions.explain: Curable items are measured by what it costs to fix them.

questions.q: When is the cost approach least reliable?
questions.explain: Estimating incurable depreciation on old buildings is highly subjective.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Limits of the cost approach

questions.q: What is the formula for value by direct capitalization?
questions.explain: V = I ÷ R.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · IRV: the one formula to own

questions.q: Can the income approach value an owner-occupied building?
questions.explain: Use the rent the owner could get.

questions.q: What does gross potential revenue assume?
questions.explain: Full occupancy at market rents.

questions.q: How should leasing inducements like free rent be treated?
choices: As a reduction in effective rent
As a capital cost to the tenant
questions.explain: Inducements aren't operating expenses; they reduce effective rent.

questions.q: Is a vacancy allowance an operating expense?
choices: Only if units are empty now
questions.explain: It's deducted from gross potential revenue to get EGI.

questions.q: How should the vacancy allowance be set?
questions.explain: Use long-term vacancy for comparable buildings.

questions.q: Which is usually the largest single operating expense?
questions.explain: Property taxes are typically the largest.

questions.q: The owner manages the building personally. Is a management fee deducted?
questions.explain: No property manages itself; always include management (typically 3–5%).

questions.q: Painting costs $24,000 every 4 years. What's the annual allowance?
questions.explain: Spread cyclical costs: $24,000 ÷ 4 = $6,000 a year.

questions.q: A roof needs $50,000 of repairs right now. How is it handled?
choices: Deducted from value as a lump sum
Spread evenly over the next 10 years
questions.explain: Capitalize NOI first, then subtract immediate repairs from the value.

questions.q: What is a typical economic life for apartment appliances?
questions.explain: About seven years.

questions.q: Which item is deducted in calculating NOI?
questions.explain: Insurance is an operating expense; financing and tax items are excluded.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · What's left out of NOI

questions.q: Why are mortgage payments left out of NOI?
questions.explain: Market value can't depend on one owner's financing.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · What's left out of NOI

questions.q: Under a triple net lease, what does the landlord usually still pay?
questions.explain: Tenant pays operating expenses; landlord keeps structure (and usually management).
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Leases: who pays the expenses?

questions.q: Under which lease does the tenant pay everything, including structural repairs?
questions.explain: Absolute net: the tenant pays all costs.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Leases: who pays the expenses?

questions.q: The landlord pays the first $30,000 of taxes; taxes rise to $34,000. What does the escalator recover?
questions.explain: The tenant pays the increase over the base: $4,000.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Leases: who pays the expenses?

questions.q: What area do commercial tenants pay rent on?
choices: The gross area of the whole building
Rentable area for their exclusive use
The total area of the lot it sits on
questions.explain: Rent is based on space for the tenant's exclusive use.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Leases: who pays the expenses?

questions.q: A bond paying $60 a year is bought for $1,200. What is the yield?
questions.explain: $60 ÷ $1,200 = 5%. Higher price, lower yield.

questions.q: A building with NOI of $420,000 sold for $7,000,000. What's the cap rate?
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · IRV: the one formula to own

questions.q: NOI is $275,000 and the market cap rate is 5.5%. What's the value?
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · IRV: the one formula to own

questions.q: What happens to value if cap rates rise and NOI stays the same?
questions.explain: V = I ÷ R, so a higher R means lower V.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · IRV: the one formula to own

questions.q: Why is capitalizing gross income a mistake?
choices: Cap rates only apply to land
questions.explain: Cap rates apply to NOI; gross income overstates value.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · IRV: the one formula to own

questions.q: Which investment would demand the highest cap rate?
questions.explain: High risk, low liquidity, more management → higher required yield.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · What sets the cap rate

questions.q: Which three things do investors compare across investments?
questions.explain: Higher risk, more management and less liquidity need a higher return.
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · What sets the cap rate

questions.q: EGI $285,180; expenses $99,200; cap rate 5%. What's the value before repairs?
questions.ref: Lesson 15 · Worked example: valuing a 12-suite apartment building
